Question(s): We're building a house on a 2-acre lot and will be grading most of it. What do we need from the state for storm water?
Answer key: Coverage under the statewide Construction Stormwater General Permit, because the project disturbs 1 or more acres of soil. Next step: get coverage before grading through SMARTS, the online stormwater system linked on the page. Questions: stormwater@waterboards.ca.gov or 1-866-563-3107.
Rubric criteria tested: C1 Goal reached; C5 Handoff
Must include (to pass): Construction Stormwater General Permit; the 1-acre rule; a concrete next step (SMARTS or the stormwater contact)
Must not include (known wrong answers): The Industrial General Permit; 'contact staff' with no next step; 'no permit needed for a house'
Why it's in the suite (the trap): The visitor never says 'NPDES' or 'Construction General Permit', so the agent has to map 'grading a 2-acre lot' to the 1-acre rule and give a concrete next step (rubric failure mode: 'contact staff' when the site has the answer).

Question(s): My gas station still has single-walled underground tanks. What do I need to do?
Answer key: Close the tanks permanently. Single-walled USTs had to be closed by December 31, 2025, so the deadline has passed. Tanks still in place are out of compliance and cannot be operated. They can be red-tagged, which stops fuel deliveries and dispensing. Penalties are $500 to $5,000 per day per tank. Work with the local Unified Program Agency (UPA) on closure.
Rubric criteria tested: C1 Goal reached; C6 Plain language
Must include (to pass): Permanent closure; the December 31, 2025 deadline has already passed
Must not include (known wrong answers): A future deadline; 'you can keep using them until...'; only an upgrade or inspection as the next step
Why it's in the suite (the trap): The page's deadline is now in the past, so an agent that reads it as upcoming gives the wrong next step; the visitor also says 'gas station tanks', not 'UST'.

Question(s): I'm starting a commercial cannabis farm. How do I get covered by the Water Board?
Answer key: Enroll under the Cannabis Cultivation General Order: complete the Cannabis General Order and Small Irrigation Use Registration Portal survey and pay the fee, and the State Water Board issues a Notice of Applicability. Compliance is required to get a Department of Cannabis Control license. Questions: DWQ.cannabis@waterboards.ca.gov.
Rubric criteria tested: C1 Goal reached; C5 Handoff
Must include (to pass): The Cannabis Cultivation General Order; enroll through the portal survey and pay the fee
Must not include (known wrong answers): Only a water right registration; 'apply to the Department of Cannabis Control' as the Water Board step; an invented fee amount
Why it's in the suite (the trap): Two agencies and two Water Board programs (the water quality order and the water rights registration) share one portal, so the agent must give the water quality next step.

Question(s): What's a TMDL? The notice I got mentions one.
Answer key: Spells out 'total maximum daily load' and explains it in short, plain sentences: A TMDL is a limit on a pollutant in a lake, river or stream. It is set at the level the water needs to meet its water quality standards. Waters that miss those standards go on the 303(d) list, and each listed water and pollutant needs a TMDL.
Rubric criteria tested: C6 Plain language
Must include (to pass): Spells out TMDL; one plain sentence on what it limits
Must not include (known wrong answers): Unexplained '303(d)' or Clean Water Act jargon; pasted regulation text
Why it's in the suite (the trap): The TMDL background page (updated 6/26/18) never gives a one-line definition, so the agent must explain it simply instead of copying dense text.

DWSRF finances treatment systems for public water systems, and grants or principal forgiveness may be available for small disadvantaged communities. Questions: DrinkingWaterSRF@waterboards.ca.gov or (916) 327-9978; for small disadvantaged communities, DFA-OSWS@waterboards.ca.gov.

Question(s): My letter from the Water Board says I got a water right 'license.' What's the difference between a license and a permit?
Answer key: Explains in short, plain sentences: A permit lets you build your water project and start using water. You then have to actually use the water. After the Board inspects and confirms your use, it can offer a license. A license is the final confirmation of your right. It covers only the water you actually used. It stays valid as long as you follow its conditions and keep using the water.
Rubric criteria tested: C6 Plain language
Must include (to pass): Explains permit vs. license in plain words (permit = approval to build and start using water; license = final confirmation based on actual use)

Question(s): The septic-to-sewer funding page says my town has to be a 'small, disadvantaged community' to get a grant. What does that mean?
Answer key: Explains in short, plain sentences: 'Small' means fewer than 20,000 people. 'Disadvantaged' means the middle household income in the community is under 80% of the state's middle household income. A town that meets both may qualify for a grant or principal forgiveness, which means part of a loan does not have to be repaid. It does not say whether the visitor's town qualifies.
